`internal/entity` is the entity registry and the engine that computes entity
state. It is the first piece of Phase 1 in [ROADMAP.md](/roadmap/): the
foundation every automation, helper, script and screen in HotLoop is built on.

## Why entities, when we already have tags

A tag is what a driver talks about: a holding register, a NodeId, an S7 DB
offset. It is keyed by device and tag name, it cannot be renamed, and it
means exactly one point on one wire.

An entity is what people and rules talk about: "the zone 1 temperature", "the
conveyor run switch". It has a stable name of its own (`sensor.zone_1_temperature`),
a type that says how to show it and what you can do to it, and a set of
bindings to the tags it is made of.

Entities wrap tags. They do not replace them, and nothing about tags changed
to make room for them. There is no second value pipeline and no second
historian: an entity's state is computed from the same live cache that
`/api/values`, the alarm engine and the OPC UA server already read. Every
existing tag endpoint, the board, `/api/write`, the MCP tools and automation
rules that existed before entities behave exactly as they did; entities are
added next to them, not in place of them.

## What you get without lifting a finger

Every tag gets a **read entity**, automatically:

| Tag data type | Read entity domain |
|---|---|
| `bool`, `boolean`, `bit`, `coil`, `discrete` | `binary_sensor` |
| everything else | `sensor` |

The first time a tag is made writable it also gets a **control entity**:

| Tag data type | Control entity domain |
|---|---|
| bool family | `switch` |
| int and float families | `number` |
| `string`, `text`, `char` | `text` |

A control entity is never removed because its tag was disarmed. The write gate
refuses writes to a disarmed tag the way it always has, and the entity's
`armed` attribute goes `false` so a screen can gray the control out. Keeping the
entity is the point: an automation or a dashboard that names
`switch.press_01_pump` should not break because somebody disarmed the pump for
a shift.

Existing tags get their entities in the upgrade itself: migration
`0005_entities.sql` backfills a read entity for every tag and a control entity
for every tag that is already writable, in the same transaction that creates
the tables. Either every tag has its entity when the new version serves its
first request, or nothing changed.

Every alarm definition gets an **alarm entity** too, the same way: see
[Alarm entities](#alarm-entities).

Commanding a control entity (turning a switch on, setting a number) is a
service call, and a service call is tag writes through `runtime.Manager.Write`
and the write gate like every other write. There is no other door. See
[Services](#services).

Equipment that is more than one tag (a pump with a run command, a running
contact and a fault; a valve with limit switches; a PID loop) is a
**composite** you build on purpose out of the tags it is made of. See
[Composite equipment](#composite-equipment).

## Entity IDs

An `entity_id` is `<domain>.<object_id>`: lowercase letters, digits and
underscores, at most 255 characters. The automatic one for a tag is
`<domain>.<device>_<tag>`, where both halves are lowercased and every run of
anything that is not an ASCII letter or digit becomes one underscore:

| Device | Tag | Read entity |
|---|---|---|
| `press-01` | `Zone1_Temp` | `sensor.press_01_zone1_temp` |
| `Line.A-2` | `Motor/Speed.PV` | `sensor.line_a_2_motor_speed_pv` |
| `press-01` | `温度` | `sensor.press_01_tag` |

Two tags that come out the same get `_2`, `_3` and so on, in the order they
were registered. A name too long for 255 characters is cut before the suffix,
never through it.

**An `entity_id` is generated once, stored, and never regenerated.** Renaming
a tag's description, changing its data type, moving it to a different
register: none of that touches the entity_id. The only thing that changes it
is an explicit rename through `PUT /api/entities/{entity_id}`, which is an admin
action and lands in the system log (category `config`, subject the new id, the
old id in the message and the detail).

A rename keeps the domain. An entity's identity is its database `id` and its
`unique_id`, and neither ever moves:

| Entity | `unique_id` |
|---|---|
| a tag's read entity | `tag:<device>/<tag>` |
| a tag's control entity | `tag-control:<device>/<tag>` |
| an alarm entity | `alarm:<definition id>` |
| a composite | `composite:<32 random hex digits>` |

The first three are derived from what the entity wraps, which is what lets a
deleted tag or alarm definition that comes back re-adopt its entity. A
composite has nothing like that to derive one from: two identical pumps on one
PLC are bound to different tags, and the same tags can back two composites on
purpose. So its `unique_id` is random, made once when it is created. It can
never collide with anything else's, including a composite that was deleted and
built again, which is a new entity and should be.

## Deleted tags, orphans and re-adoption

Delete a tag and its entities are **orphaned**, not deleted: `orphaned_at` is
set and the state goes `unavailable`. Bring the same tag back, by the tag
editor or by a browse re-import, and the registry finds the orphan by
`unique_id` and re-adopts it. Its entity_id, name, device class, icon and every
other customization come back with it.

That is deliberate. On a plant floor a tag gets deleted and re-imported far
more often than anybody means "forget everything about this point", and an
automation naming `sensor.oven_temperature` should keep working across it.

Deleting a whole device is different: its entities go with it, the same way
its tags do. That includes a composite whose tags are all on that device. A
composite spanning several devices belongs to none of them, and loses nothing
but its state when one goes.

Alarm entities follow their alarm definitions by the same rules: delete the
definition and its entity is orphaned, save a definition with the same id and
it is re-adopted.

A composite is never orphaned. It was built on purpose, so it stays until
somebody deletes it; while one of its tags is gone it is `unavailable`.

`DELETE /api/entities/{entity_id}` deletes a composite, or an orphan. It
refuses (409) a tag's or an alarm definition's entity that still has what it
wraps, and says how it goes away: delete the tag or the definition, then the
orphan. Deleting a live one would only have the next sync put it back under a
new id, and break everything naming it in between. To take one off screens,
hide or disable it.

## How the registry keeps up

The registry does not hook each place a tag can change. It reconciles: read
every tag and every entity, create what is missing, orphan what lost its tag,
re-adopt what got it back. A reconcile cannot miss a path somebody adds next
year, and running it twice is running it once. It runs:

- on start, which covers an upgrade and a restore from backup;
- after every runtime reload, which every tag and device change already
  triggers;
- synchronously in the API handlers that change tags (`POST /api/tags`,
  `DELETE /api/tags/...`, `POST /api/devices/{id}/import`,
  `DELETE /api/devices/{id}`) and alarm definitions (`POST /api/alarms`,
  `DELETE /api/alarms/{id}`), so a client that creates a tag or a definition
  and immediately asks for its entity finds it.

Registration is serialized across replicas with a database advisory lock, so
two replicas importing the same device cannot hand out the same `_2`. Each
reconcile that changes something writes one line to the system log, not one
per entity: an import of five thousand points is one event.

## State

`GET /api/states/{entity_id}`:

```json
{
  "entity_id": "sensor.press_01_zone1_temp",
  "state": "212.5",
  "attributes": {
    "friendly_name": "Zone1_Temp",
    "unit_of_measurement": "F",
    "device_class": "temperature",
    "source": ["press-01/Zone1_Temp"]
  },
  "quality": "good",
  "last_changed": "2026-09-26T14:02:11.482Z",
  "last_updated": "2026-09-26T14:02:11.482Z",
  "last_reported": "2026-09-26T14:07:40.100Z"
}
```

`state` is the value rendered without its unit: a number the way `/api/values`
displays it, `on` or `off` for `binary_sensor` and `switch`, the text itself for
a string. The unit is an attribute. A state that is sometimes `212.5` and
sometimes `212.5 F` is a state nothing can compare.

The rules, in the order they are applied. They are the same rules the OPC UA
server uses for its status codes, for the same reason: **a state is never
better than the evidence for it.**

| Condition | `state` | `quality` |
|---|---|---|
| Entity orphaned, or its tag is gone | `unavailable` | `bad` |
| Device disabled, deleted, or its link is not up | `unavailable` | `bad` |
| Link up, nothing read yet in this session | `unknown` | `bad` |
| Bad reading | the **last good value**, or `unknown` if there never was one | `bad` |
| Good reading, but other points on the device are failing (degraded) | the value | `uncertain` |
| Good reading | the value | `good` |

The bad-reading rule matters more than it looks. A driver reports a point it
could not read as a bad reading of zero, and showing that zero as the state
turns "the level transmitter stopped answering" into "the tank is empty". The
entity keeps showing the last value it could trust and says, in `quality`, that
it can no longer vouch for it.

Note the difference between a point failing and a device failing. A Modbus
device whose every block fails drops its session and reconnects, so its
entities go `unavailable`. A device that answers for some points and not
others stays connected (degraded), and only the failing points' entities show
`bad`.

**How fast a dead Modbus device shows.** One that refuses or closes the
connection is `unavailable` by its next poll. One that simply stops answering
(a pulled cable, a hung PLC, a switch that rebooted) keeps its socket open and
is judged by its poll timeout instead: its entities are `unavailable` within
one poll interval plus twice the device's timeout, plus at most a second for
the engine's backstop recompute. Usually it is one timeout; twice is when the
device dies while a poll is part way through, because the request already on
the wire gets its full timeout. Until then nothing new has been read, so the
entity still shows its last reading as it was. A hung device that still
accepts connections is reconnected straight away, so after that its entities
alternate between `unavailable` and `unknown` (connected, nothing read) until
it answers again; neither is ever mistaken for a value. The timeout is the
knob: a device on a 20 second timeout can look fine for 20 to 40 seconds after
it dies, so do not set it longer than the device needs to answer.

That table is for entities of one tag. A composite is stricter (a bad reading
never keeps its last value, see [How a composite's state is
decided](#how-a-composites-state-is-decided)), and an alarm entity's state is
the alarm engine's (see [Alarm entities](#alarm-entities)).

### Timestamps

- `last_changed` moves only when `state` changes.
- `last_updated` moves when `state`, `quality` or any attribute changes.
- `last_reported` is the timestamp of the reading the state came from. It is
  absent until there is one.

State is computed, not stored, but the logbook keeps every entity's newest
state and when it last changed (`entity_last_state`, see
[LOGBOOK.md](/iot/logbook/)). After a restart, an entity whose state comes back
the same **keeps its `last_changed`**: a pump running since Tuesday still says
Tuesday. The unavailable and unknown a tag entity passes through while its
device reconnects do not count as a change. A state that did change while the
Gateway was down gets a fresh `last_changed`, and a line in the logbook.
Numeric entities (sensors, numbers, loops, counters) and buttons are not
tracked, so theirs, like every entity's `last_updated`, starts again from the
restart.

### Attributes

Every entity carries `friendly_name` and `source` (the tag keys it is bound
to). Then, when they apply:

| Attribute | When |
|---|---|
| `unit_of_measurement` | `sensor` and `number`: the entity's own unit, or its tag's |
| `device_class`, `state_class`, `icon` | when set on the entity |
| `armed` | control entities: whether the tag is writable right now |
| `min`, `max` | `number`: the entity's options, else the tag's range if it has one |
| `step` | `number`: the entity's option, else 1 for an integer tag |
| `max_length`, `pattern` | `text`: the entity's options, `max_length` defaulting to 255 |
| `quality_reason` | tag entities, while the reading isn't good and the driver knows why: `no field at ENERGY.Power`, `payload is not JSON`. Gone again with the next good reading |

### Disabled and hidden

A **disabled** entity has no state at all: it is absent from `/api/states`,
and asking for it by id says it is disabled rather than missing. A **hidden**
entity has its state as usual; the flag is for screens to leave it off default
views.

### How the engine runs

The engine subscribes to the tag bus as `entities` with a queue of 256
batches, the same lossy contract as the alarm and automation engines: a slow
consumer loses batches, it never stalls a poll. A dropped batch here costs at
most a second, because the engine also recomputes every entity from the cache
once a second. That tick is also what catches changes nothing announces, such
as a device's first poll landing.

Subscribers inside the process register with `Engine.OnStateChanged`. They
are called on the engine's own goroutine, in the order the changes happened,
which is what a rule that cares about "from X to Y" needs. They must be quick.
The engine never waits for them; if they fall more than 10,000 changes
behind, the oldest are dropped and counted.

`GET /api/diagnostics` reports it under `entities`:

| Field | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `entities` | how many entities have a state |
| `droppedBatches` | bus batches the engine was too slow to take (also under `bus.droppedPerSubscriber.entities`) |
| `pendingChanges`, `droppedChanges` | the state-change hook queue. A growing backlog, or any drop, means a hook is too slow |

## Device classes and units

A device class says what a value is (`temperature`, `pressure`,
`volume_flow_rate`, `running`, `problem`) so a screen can pick an icon and a
statistics consumer knows what to do with it. Each class has the units it
usually comes in. The full table is `model.DeviceClasses`.

- An unknown device class for the domain is refused.
- A unit the class does not usually have is **saved, with a warning** in the
  response. Plants label things the way plants label things, and `degF` on a
  temperature is not worth blocking a save over. Plain `F` and `C` are accepted
  for temperature without a warning, because that is what most PLC tag
  databases actually carry.
- `state_class` (`measurement`, `total`, `total_increasing`) is for sensors
  only.
- **There is no unit conversion.** The unit is a label.

## API

Entity endpoints use snake_case field names (`entity_id`,
`last_changed`) rather than this API's usual camelCase. That is on purpose: the
entity API exists so that anything which already understands that shape
understands this one.

| Endpoint | Permission | What |
|---|---|---|
| `GET /api/entities` | `entities.read` | Every entity, orphans included. Filters: `?domain=`, `?device=`, `?orphaned=true\|false` |
| `GET /api/entities/{entity_id}` | `entities.read` | `{"entity": ..., "state": ...}`; `state` is null for a disabled entity |
| `GET /api/entities/{entity_id}/image` | `entities.read` | a camera's or an image's latest picture |
| `PUT /api/entities/{entity_id}` | `entities.write` | Change registry fields, including a rename. Answers `{"entity": ..., "warnings": [...]}` |
| `POST /api/entities` | `entities.write` | Create a composite. Answers 201 `{"entity": ..., "warnings": [...]}`. See [Composite equipment](#composite-equipment) |
| `DELETE /api/entities/{entity_id}` | `entities.write` | Delete a composite or an orphan. Anything else is 409 |
| `GET /api/states` | `entities.read` | Every enabled entity's state, ordered by entity_id. Filter: `?domain=` |
| `GET /api/states/{entity_id}` | `entities.read` | One state |
| `POST /api/services/{domain}/{service}` | `values.write` (`alarms.ack` for `alarm`) | Call a service on one entity. See [Services](#services). `?dry_run=true` asks what it would do instead; see [Asking first](#asking-first-the-dry-run) |
| `GET /api/writes?entity={entity_id}` | `values.read` | Every write service calls made or had refused on one entity, newest first |

Every role holds `entities.read`: an entity's state is a tag's value under
another name, which a viewer can already read. Only admin holds
`entities.write`: the entity_id is the name every automation, dashboard and
agent refers to the entity by, and changing it is configuration, not
operation.

A `PUT` body changes only the fields it names. Unknown fields are refused, and
so are the identity fields (`unique_id`, `domain`, `platform`, the device and
the bindings):

```json
{
  "entity_id": "sensor.zone_1_temperature",
  "name": "Zone 1 temperature",
  "device_class": "temperature",
  "state_class": "measurement",
  "unit_of_measurement": "°F",
  "icon": "mdi:thermometer",
  "entity_category": "",
  "options": {},
  "disabled": false,
  "hidden": false
}
```

`options` takes `min`, `max` and `step` on a `number` (they narrow what a
screen offers; the write gate still checks the tag's own range regardless) and
`max_length` and `pattern` on a `text`. A composite's options are its own (see
each domain below), and a `PUT` that changes them is checked against its tags
exactly as the create was. `sensor`, `binary_sensor`, `switch` and `alarm`
take none.

An entity also has a place on the equipment tree and a set of labels:
`equipment_id` (null to follow its device), the read-only `area_id` clients
group by, and `labels`. `PUT` takes `equipment_id` and `labels` like any
other field. See [EQUIPMENT.md](/iot/equipment/).

## Services

A service is what you can do to an entity: `switch.turn_on`,
`number.set_value`. It names the thing you want done to the entity, and
underneath it is nothing but tag writes.

```
POST /api/services/switch/turn_on
{"entity_id": "switch.press_01_pump", "reason": "start of shift"}

POST /api/services/number/set_value
{"entity_id": "number.press_01_zone1_sp", "value": 212.5}
```

The body is `entity_id`, an optional `reason`, and the service data. One
entity per call, never a list, because the answer to "what went out" should
be about one entity.

### What each domain takes

| Service | Data | Writes |
|---|---|---|
| `switch.turn_on`, `switch.turn_off` | none | `true` or `false` to the command tag |
| `switch.toggle` | none | the opposite of the current state, read from the live cache by the same rules as the state itself. If the state is `unknown`, `unavailable` or bad quality, the call is refused: toggling something whose state you do not know is guessing which way to move it. Say `turn_on` or `turn_off` |
| `number.set_value` | `value`, a number | the value, to the command tag |
| `text.set_value` | `value`, a string | the string, to the command tag |
| `select.select_option` | `option` | the option's raw value, to the command tag |
| `button.press` | none | `press_value`, then `pulse_ms` later `release_value`, to the command tag; a `single_shot` button writes `press_value` once and nothing after |
| `motor.start`, `motor.stop` | none | `true` or `false` to `run_command` |
| `motor.reset` | none | a pulse on `reset_command`: `true`, then `pulse_ms` later `false` |
| `motor.set_speed` | `value`, a number | the value, to `speed_command` |
| `valve.open`, `valve.close` | none | `true` or `false` to `command`; on a modulating valve, 100 or 0 to `position_command` |
| `valve.stop` | none | a pulse on `stop_command`; a `single_shot` valve writes `true` once |
| `valve.set_position` | `position`, 0 to 100 | the position, to `position_command` |
| `loop.set_setpoint` | `value`, a number | the value, to `setpoint` |
| `loop.set_mode` | `mode`: `auto`, `manual` or `cascade` | the mode's raw value, to `mode` |
| `loop.set_output` | `value`, a number | the value, to `output`, **only while the loop reads manual** |
| `counter.reset` | none | 0 to a numeric `reset_command`, or a pulse on a bool one |
| `alarm.acknowledge` | `note`, optional | no tag: the alarm engine's acknowledge |
| `alarm.shelve` | `minutes`, 1 to 1440 | no tag: the alarm engine's shelve |
| `alarm.unshelve` | none | no tag: the alarm engine's unshelve, only on a shelved alarm |
| `script.turn_on` | the script's fields | no tag itself: runs the [script](/iot/scripts/), whose steps write through the gate as `script:<id>` |
| `script.turn_off` | none | no tag: stops every run of the script |
| `scene.turn_on` | `params`, the recipe's parameters, and `version`, both optional | no tag itself: applies the [recipe](/iot/recipes/), whose targets write through the gate under one call id |
| `light.turn_on` | `brightness`, 0 to 100, optional | `true` to `command`, then the brightness to `brightness_command` |
| `light.turn_off` | none | `false` to `command` |
| `light.toggle` | none | the opposite of what the light's state feedback says; refused when that can't be read |
| `cover.open`, `cover.close`, `cover.stop` | none | `open`, `close` or `stop` to `command` |
| `cover.set_position` | `position`, 0 to 100 | the position, to `position_command` |
| `lock.lock`, `lock.unlock`, `lock.open` | none | `lock`, `unlock` or `open` to `state` |
| `fan.turn_on` | `percentage`, `preset_mode`, both optional | `true` to `state`, then each one given |
| `fan.turn_off`, `fan.toggle` | none | `false`, or the opposite of what its feedback says, to `state` |
| `fan.set_percentage` | `percentage`, 0 to 100 | to `percentage` |
| `fan.set_preset_mode`, `fan.set_direction` | `preset_mode`, `direction` | to `preset_mode`, `direction` |
| `fan.oscillate` | `oscillating`, true or false | to `oscillating` |
| `siren.turn_on`, `siren.turn_off`, `siren.toggle` | none | like a switch, to `state` |
| `notify.send_message` | `message` | the message, to `message` |

A composite service whose role is not bound (`set_speed` on a motor with no
`speed_command`) is refused before anything is planned, as an unknown service.

`sensor` and `binary_sensor` are read-only and take no services. Service data
with a field the service does not take is refused, the same way a misspelled
field in any other body is: a call that quietly goes ahead without the field
you meant is worse than one that says no.

A number that is a whole number reaches an integer tag as an integer: `42.0`
is `42`.

### Every call goes through the write gate

A service call becomes an ordered list of writes, and every one goes through
`runtime.Manager.Write`. So everything the gate enforces on a write to a tag,
it enforces on a service call, in the same order:

1. writes enabled (`safety.allowWrites`), and for an agent, agent writes
   enabled;
2. the tag armed (`writable`);
3. the value inside the tag's range, rejected, never clamped;
4. then what only the entity knows, checked inside the gate against the
   entity and the tag as they are at that moment:
   - the entity is not disabled (commanding something that has no state is
     not allowed);
   - a `number`'s own `min` and `max`, which can only narrow the tag's range;
   - a `number`'s `step`, counted from its minimum (its own, else the tag's
     range minimum, else zero). An integer tag has a step of 1 unless the
     entity says otherwise, so `1.5` to a holding register is refused instead
     of a driver quietly truncating it to `1`;
   - a `text`'s `max_length` (characters, 255 when unset) and its `pattern`,
     which the whole value must match;
   - a `select` option or a loop mode that is not one of the entity's. It is
     sent to the gate as the option or mode asked for, and refused there, so
     somebody trying options that do not exist is on the record;
   - a valve position outside 0 to 100;
   - a loop's `set_output` while its mode tag, read from the live cache at
     that moment, is anything but manual (auto, cascade, a value that is none
     of the modes, or unreadable).

Every refusal, at any of those steps, is **audited**: a `write_audit` row with
the entity, the service and the call id on it, `succeeded` false and the reason
starting `refused:`. That includes a user without `values.write`. The API does
not just answer 403 and forget it: it sends the call to the gate marked denied,
the gate refuses it before anything is written, and the refusal is on the
entity's record with the value that was asked for. A write straight to a tag
through `POST /api/write` behaves exactly as it always did, byte for byte;
`TestPostWriteIsByteIdenticalToBeforeEntityServices` holds it there.

Nothing in `internal/entity` can reach a device any other way. It does not
import a driver, and `TestOnlyTheGateCallsWorkerWrite` type-checks the runtime
and fails the build if anything but `Manager.Write` calls the worker's write,
or anything but that calls a driver's. It matches the shape of a device write,
not a name, so a bypass through a new wrapper or an interface declared on the
spot is caught too. `TestGateGuardCatchesABypass` plants each of those in a
copy of the package to prove the guard can fail.

### What a call answers

```json
{
  "call_id": "9f2c4e1a7b3d5c60",
  "entity_id": "switch.press_01_pump",
  "service": "switch.turn_on",
  "writes": [
    {"tag": "press-01/pump", "value": "true", "status": "written"}
  ]
}
```

Each write has a status:

| Status | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `written` | the device accepted it |
| `not_sent` | the gate turned it away before it reached the device: a refusal, no session, an audit row that could not be opened |
| `failed` | it went out and the device or the connection reported an error. Whether it took is not known |
| `skipped` | never attempted, because an earlier write in the same call did not succeed |

A failed call answers with the error's status code (403 refused by policy or
permission, 422 a value refused, 409 a toggle with no known state or equipment
in the wrong state for the service, 503 the device not connected, 502 the
device took the write and reported an error, 404 no such entity, 400 a
malformed call, 500 a press whose release did not go through, or a fault inside
the Gateway, whose `error` is only a reference to the server log) and the same
body with `error` added.

The writes of one call go out in order, the first that does not succeed ends
the call, and **nothing already written is rolled back**. Undoing is itself a
write, made without anybody asking for it, to equipment that has already
moved. Deciding that is the operator's job, and the answer tells them exactly
where the call stopped. Every write of one call shares its `call_id`, in the
audit trail and in the answer.

There is one exception, and it is the momentary command: a button's press, a
motor's reset, a valve's stop, a counter's reset on a bit. Those are two
writes, the press and pulse_ms later the release, and the release is not
something to skip lightly, because skipping it leaves a pushbutton held down.
So:

- The release is still sent when the press went out and reported an error
  (`failed`): it may have taken. It is skipped only when the press was
  `not_sent`, because then nothing is held.
- The release is sent even if the caller hangs up during the pulse. The call
  carries on without it.
- If the press was written and the release was refused or failed, the call
  fails with a 500 and says so: the tag **may still hold the press value**,
  check it and release it by hand. The release's refusal or failure is in the
  audit trail under the same call id, and the call is logged under the entity
  at severity error, not warning.

A pulse is `pulse_ms` long, 500 by default, at most 10,000. The call answers
when the release is done, so a caller waits for the pulse.

Each call is also one line in the system log, under the entity_id, category
`write`, with the reason and, in the detail, the call id, the source and every
write with its status. The individual tag writes keep their own lines under
their tags, as they always have.

`GET /api/writes?entity=switch.press_01_pump` is that entity's audit trail,
refusals included, newest first. The rows have `entityId`, `service` and
`callId`; a write straight to a tag leaves them out, so every existing reader of
`/api/writes` sees exactly what it saw before. Migration
`0007_service_audit.sql` adds the three columns, empty for every existing row.

### Asking first: the dry run

`POST /api/services/{domain}/{service}?dry_run=true` asks the gate what it would
do with a call, and does none of it. Same body, same permission.

```json
{"dry_run":true,"entity_id":"number.press_01_zone1_sp","service":"number.set_value","writes":[{"tag":"press-01/zone1_sp","value":"212.5","status":"would_write"}]}
```

```json
{"dry_run":true,"error":"press-01/zone1_sp: this tag is not marked writable","entity_id":"number.press_01_zone1_sp","service":"number.set_value","writes":[{"tag":"press-01/zone1_sp","value":"212.5","status":"not_sent","error":"press-01/zone1_sp: this tag is not marked writable"}]}
```

The call is planned exactly as the real one is, and every write it would make
is put to the gate's own checks, in the same order, against the tags, the
entity and the device as they are right now: writes on, the agent switch, the
tag armed, its range, everything only the entity knows (step, pattern, a loop
in manual, a disabled entity), and a session to the device. The first write
that would be refused is `not_sent` with the reason, the rest `skipped`, and
`error` is the error the real call would fail with, **word for word**. A write
that would go out is `would_write`. It is one function in the gate
(`precheck`) answering both, so a dry run cannot pass on checks the real write
does not make. An `alarm` entity writes no tag, so its dry run makes the alarm
checks instead (the engine running, the definition still there, the entity
enabled, only a shelved alarm unshelved) and answers with no writes; the alarm
is not touched and the alarm trail gets nothing.

It is a question, so a verdict, refused or not, answers 200. A request the real
call would turn away before any check (no such entity, a service the domain
does not take, data it does not accept, a toggle with no known state, the
wrong domain in the path) answers with the same status and error the real call
would. A user without the permission gets the same 403.

A dry run writes nothing, opens no audit row, puts nothing in the system log
and spends no call id: nothing was attempted, so there is nothing to account
for. `TestCheckWriteCannotReachTheDeviceOrTheAudit` walks every function the
gate's dry run can reach and fails if the device write, the audit or the log is
among them; `TestCheckAnswersExactlyWhatTheCallWould` runs each refusal a plant
relies on as a dry run and then for real against a Modbus device and holds the
two to the same words.

It says what would happen **right now**. Between the dry run and the real call
the device can drop and somebody can disarm the tag; the real call is checked
again, in full, at the moment of the write. One case is answered more
precisely than the real call's own checks: a device whose session has dropped
while its worker reconnects. The real write gets as far as the driver and fails
there (`failed`, 503, and an audit row for the attempt); the dry run says
`not_sent` up front, with the same error.

The command prompt on the Entities screen and in the entity drawer uses it: as
the prompt opens and as a value is typed, it asks, and a refusal shows in the
prompt, in the gate's words, before anybody presses confirm. It is advice, not a
lock: confirm still goes to the gate, which decides again.

## Composite equipment

A tag maps onto one entity. A pump does not map onto one tag: it has a run
command, a running contact, a fault, a reset and maybe a speed, and the
operator thinks of it as one thing. A composite is that one thing, bound to each
of its tags in a named **role**.

An admin builds one with `POST /api/entities`:

```json
{
  "domain": "motor",
  "name": "Infeed pump",
  "device_class": "pump",
  "options": {"pulse_ms": 500},
  "bindings": [
    {"role": "running",       "device_id": "press-01", "tag_name": "P101_Running"},
    {"role": "run_command",   "device_id": "press-01", "tag_name": "P101_RunCmd"},
    {"role": "fault",         "device_id": "press-01", "tag_name": "P101_Fault"},
    {"role": "reset_command", "device_id": "press-01", "tag_name": "P101_Reset"}
  ]
}
```

`entity_id` is optional. Leave it out and one is made from the name
(`motor.infeed_pump`, then `_2` and so on). Give it and it is used exactly, and
a taken one is a 409, not a quiet `_2`: you asked for that name. `name`,
`device_class`, `unit_of_measurement`, `icon`, `entity_category` and `options`
are the same registry fields every entity has. Place it on the equipment tree
and label it with `PUT` afterwards.

Creation checks everything it can against the tags as they are now, and
refuses (400, saying what to fix) anything that is not right:

- the domain is one of `select`, `button`, `motor`, `valve`, `loop`,
  `counter`. The tag domains are made for you from tags, and `alarm` from alarm
  definitions;
- every required role is bound, and no role the domain does not have;
- **every bound tag exists**;
- **every tag's type fits its role**: a motor's `running` is a bool, a valve's
  `position` is a number, a counter's count is an integer;
- **every tag a service writes is already armed** (`writable`). A composite
  never arms anything. Arming a point stays a decision somebody makes about the
  tag, one at a time, the same as it always was;
- every raw value in the options (a select option's value, a button's press and
  release values, a loop's modes) is one its tag can take. `1.5` is refused for
  an integer register now, not when somebody presses the button.

A composite goes with its device when all its tags are on one device, and
belongs to none when they span several. Its bindings are fixed: a different set
of tags is a different entity, so delete it and build another.

Every creation and deletion is one line in the system log under the entity_id,
category `config`, with the bindings.

### Roles

| Domain | Role | Tag type | <span class="sr-only">Details</span> |
|---|---|---|---|
| `select` | `state` | any | required. Feedback: read back to find the option |
| | `command` | any | required, armed. Written with the option's raw value. May be the same tag as `state` |
| `button` | `command` | any | required, armed. Pulsed |
| `motor` | `running` | bool | required. Feedback: the running contact |
| | `run_command` | bool | required, armed. `start` writes true, `stop` false |
| | `fault` | bool | feedback |
| | `reset_command` | bool | armed. Pulsed by `reset` |
| | `speed` | number | feedback, the `speed` attribute |
| | `speed_command` | number | armed. Written by `set_speed` |
| `valve` | `state` | any | feedback: where a valve that announced itself says it is, in words |
| | `opened`, `closed` | bool | feedback: the limit switches |
| | `position` | number | feedback, 0 to 100 percent |
| | `fault` | bool | feedback |
| | `command` | bool | armed. An on/off valve: `open` writes true, `close` false |
| | `position_command` | number | armed. A modulating valve: `set_position`, and `open`/`close` as 100/0 |
| | `stop_command` | bool | armed. Pulsed by `stop` |
| `loop` | `pv` | number | required. The state |
| | `setpoint` | number | required, armed. Read for the attribute, written by `set_setpoint` |
| | `output` | number | required, armed. Read for the attribute, written by `set_output` |
| | `mode` | any | required, armed. Read to know the mode, written by `set_mode` |
| `counter` | `state` | integer | required. The count |
| | `reset_command` | bool or number | armed. Pulsed if a bool, written with 0 if a number (it may be the count register itself) |

A valve needs at least one of `state`, `opened`, `closed` and `position` (something has
to say where it is) and exactly one of `command` and `position_command`. Both
at once would be two answers to "where has it been told to go", and the state
between the limits depends on that answer. If the PLC really has both, make two
entities.

### Options

| Option | Domain | <span class="sr-only">Details</span> |
|---|---|---|
| `select_options` | `select` | required: `[{"option": "low", "value": 1}, ...]`, in the order a screen offers them. Names unique, values unique (two options with one value would make the state a guess), each value a number, a bool or a string |
| `press_value`, `release_value` | `button` | together or not at all. Left out on a bool tag, they are `true` and `false`, written into the options so what the button does is on the record. Any other tag type needs both |
| `pulse_ms` | `button`, `motor`, `valve`, `counter` | how long a momentary command is held. 1 to 10,000, 500 when unset |
| `single_shot` | `button`, `valve` | `true` writes `press_value` once and never releases: the press is the whole command. A discovered MQTT button is one, because its "release" would be a second command the device never asked for. Takes `press_value` and no `release_value` or `pulse_ms`. On a valve, its `stop` writes `true` once instead of a pulse: a discovered valve's stop is a command of its own |
| `event_types` | `event` | the event types it can fire, when it says |
| `role_choices` | `lock`, `fan`, `siren`, `notify`, `update`, `device_tracker`, `climate`, `humidifier`, `water_heater` | the words each commanded role offers, by role, 1 to 64 distinct each: a thermostat's modes. Discovery sets it from the config |
| `modes` | `loop` | required: the raw value of the mode tag for each mode, `{"auto": 1, "manual": 0}` at least, `cascade` if the controller has it |

### How a composite's state is decided

A composite's state comes from its **feedback**. It is never computed from the
fact that HotLoop sent a command. A motor told to start whose running contact
has not made is not running, it is starting, and if the contact never makes it
stays starting until somebody looks. The read-back of a command tag does count
as feedback: that is the PLC saying what it holds, not HotLoop remembering what
it wrote.

A composite is **never optimistic**. A single sensor keeps showing its last good
value through a bad reading; a composite does not. Every feedback role that
decides the state must have a good reading, or:

| Condition | `state` | `quality` |
|---|---|---|
| a deciding tag is gone, or its device is down | `unavailable` | `bad` |
| a deciding tag has no reading yet, or a bad one | `unknown` | `bad` |
| every deciding tag good, one of them uncertain or on a degraded device | the state | `uncertain` |
| every deciding tag good | the state | `good` |

A motor whose fault input stopped answering is `unknown`, not the `running` it
was a second ago. Which roles decide is below; the others only fill attributes,
and an unreadable one is simply left out.

A composite's `armed` attribute is true only when every tag any of its services
writes is armed right now. A motor that can be started but not stopped from
here is not one a screen should offer.

### `motor`

Deciding roles: `running`, and `fault` if bound. State, first rule that
matches:

1. `fault` on: **`fault`**, whatever else is true. Running and fault together
   is contradictory, and the one that needs a person is the fault; the
   `running` attribute still says it is turning.
2. running, and the run command reads back off: **`stopping`**.
3. running: **`running`**.
4. not running, and the run command reads back on: **`starting`**.
5. otherwise: **`stopped`**.

If the run command's read-back is unreadable it decides nothing: the motor is
then `running` or `stopped` by its contact alone. HotLoop does not time out a
start that never makes: that is a fail-to-start, and it belongs in the PLC or
in an alarm definition on the running contact.

Attributes: `running`, `fault` (if bound), `command` (the read-back), `speed`
(if bound and readable), `device_class` (`pump`, `fan`, `conveyor`,
`compressor`, `agitator`).

### `valve`

A valve that announced itself (MQTT discovery) says where it is in words on its
`state` role: `open`, `closed`, `opening`, `closing` or `stopped`, and that is
its state, with `current_position` from `position` when it reports one. A word
that is none of those is `unknown`, with what it said in `raw_value`. The rest
of this section is a valve built from PLC tags.

Deciding roles: every bound one of `opened`, `closed`, `position`, `fault`.
State, first rule that matches:

1. `fault` on: **`fault`**.
2. both limit switches made: **`fault`**, with `limit_conflict: true`. A valve
   cannot be open and closed, so one switch is lying, and which one is not
   something to guess.
3. open limit made: **`open`**. Closed limit made: **`closed`**.
4. no limit switches, only a position: at or below 1% **`closed`**, at or above
   99% **`open`**.
5. between the ends, traveling or stopped by what it is commanded to: a
   position command read back more than 1% above the position is
   **`opening`**, more than 1% below **`closing`**, within 1% **`stopped`**; an
   on/off command read back on is **`opening`**, off is **`closing`**; with
   nothing to go by, **`stopped`**.

An on/off valve stopped between its limits while still commanded open reads
`opening`. If you need to see it stopped there, bind `position`.

`current_position` is the position feedback when bound, else 100 on the open
limit and 0 on the closed one, and absent in between. Other attributes:
`open_limit`, `closed_limit`, `fault`, `device_class` (`water`, `gas`, `steam`,
`air`).

### `loop`

The state is the process variable, rendered like a sensor's, from `pv` alone.
The attributes are `setpoint` and `output` (present when readable), `mode` (the
name of the mode the mode tag reads, or `unknown` when it cannot be read or
holds a value that is none of the modes), `modes` (the configured names), and
`unit_of_measurement` (the entity's, else the PV tag's). A loop takes the
sensor device classes: a temperature loop, a pressure loop.

`set_output` is refused inside the gate unless the loop reads manual **at the
moment of the write**. An output written to a loop in auto fights the
controller, and in cascade it fights two. A mode that cannot be read is not
manual. The refusal is a `write_audit` row like any other, with the entity, the
service, the call id and the value asked for, and the call answers 409. Put the
loop in manual with `set_mode` first.

### `counter`

The state is the count, an integer tag. `reset` writes 0 to a numeric
`reset_command` (bind the count register itself if that is how the PLC resets
it) or pulses a bool one. A counter with no `reset_command` is read-only.
`unit_of_measurement` is the entity's, else the tag's.

### `select`

The state is the option whose raw value the `state` tag reads. A value that is
none of the options is `unknown`, with the raw value in `raw_value`, rather than
the nearest option or the last one. The `options` attribute lists the option
names in order. An option that is not one of the select's is refused in the
gate and audited with the option that was asked for.

### `button`

A button has no feedback. Its state is the time of its last press through this
Gateway, or `unknown` if it has not been pressed since the Gateway started.
It is `unavailable` when its command tag is gone or its device is down,
because pressing it then cannot work. The last press is
held in memory, so it resets on a restart; the audit trail has every press
regardless, which is also why the logbook does not log a button's state.

## Lights, covers and events

Made by [MQTT discovery](/iot/mqtt-discovery/) for a device that announced one, bound
to the tags discovery made for it. Nobody builds these out of PLC tags, so
`POST /api/entities` doesn't take them. Same rules as every composite: the
state is what the feedback says, never what HotLoop last sent, and every
service is writes through the gate, each tag armed by a person first.

| Domain | Role | Tag type | <span class="sr-only">Details</span> |
|---|---|---|---|
| `light` | `state` | bool | feedback: on or off |
| | `command` | bool | armed. `turn_on` writes true, `turn_off` false. The same tag as `state` |
| | `brightness` | number | feedback, 0 to 100 percent, the `brightness` attribute |
| | `brightness_command` | number | armed. `turn_on` with a `brightness`. The same tag as `brightness` |
| `cover` | `state` | any | feedback: `open`, `closed`, `opening`, `closing` or `stopped` |
| | `command` | any | armed. `open`, `close` or `stop`. The same tag as `state` |
| | `position` | number | feedback, 0 (closed) to 100 (open), `current_position` |
| | `position_command` | number | armed. `set_position`. The same tag as `position` |
| `event` | `state` | any | the event type it last fired |
| `lock` | `state` | any | read and written: `locked`, `unlocked`, `locking`, `unlocking`, `jammed`, `open`, `opening`; takes `lock`, `unlock`, `open` |
| `fan` | `state` | bool | read and written: on or off |
| | `percentage` | number | read and written, 0 to 100 |
| | `preset_mode`, `direction` | any | read and written |
| | `oscillating` | bool | read and written |
| `siren` | `state` | bool | read and written: on or off |
| `notify` | `message` | any | written: the message. Nothing to read |
| `update` | `installed_version`, `latest_version` | any | read |
| `device_tracker` | `state` | any | read: `home`, `not_home`, or the zone it names |
| `climate` | `mode` | any | read and written: the state. `set_hvac_mode` with `hvac_mode` |
| | `temperature`, `target_temp_low`, `target_temp_high` | number | read and written. `set_temperature` with any of them |
| | `target_humidity` | number | read and written. `set_humidity` with `humidity` |
| | `fan_mode`, `swing_mode`, `swing_horizontal_mode`, `preset_mode` | any | read and written, each by its own `set_` service |
| | `current_temperature`, `current_humidity`, `action` | number, number, any | read |
| | `power` | bool | written: `turn_on` true, `turn_off` false. Nothing to read |
| `humidifier` | `state` | bool | read and written: on or off |
| | `target_humidity` | number | read and written. `set_humidity` with `humidity` |
| | `mode` | any | read and written. `set_mode` with `mode` |
| | `current_humidity`, `action` | number, any | read |
| `water_heater` | `mode` | any | read and written: the state. `set_operation_mode` with `operation_mode` |
| | `temperature` | number | read and written. `set_temperature` |
| | `current_temperature` | number | read |
| | `power` | bool | written: `turn_on`, `turn_off` |
| `alarm_control_panel` | `state` | any | read: `disarmed`, `armed_home`, `armed_away`, `armed_night`, `armed_vacation`, `armed_custom_bypass`, `pending`, `triggered`, `arming`, `disarming`; written by `alarm_arm_home`, `alarm_arm_away`, `alarm_arm_night`, `alarm_arm_vacation`, `alarm_arm_custom_bypass`, `alarm_disarm`, `alarm_trigger` |
| `vacuum` | `state` | any | read: `cleaning`, `docked`, `paused`, `idle`, `returning`, `error`; written by `start`, `pause`, `stop`, `return_to_base`, `clean_spot`, `locate` |
| | `battery_level` | number | read |
| | `fan_speed` | any | read and written. `set_fan_speed` with `fan_speed` |
| `lawn_mower` | `activity` | any | read: `mowing`, `paused`, `docked`, `error`, `returning` |
| `camera` | `image` | any | read: a hash of the latest picture. The state is when it changed; `entity_picture` is where to get it |
| `image` | `image` or `url` | any | read: a held picture as for a camera, or a link (`url`, http or https only, never fetched) |
| | `start_mowing`, `pause`, `dock` | bool | written: a press each, by the service of the same name |

A lock, a fan, a siren, a notifier, an update, a tracker, a thermostat, a
humidifier, a water heater, an alarm panel, a vacuum and a mower are one table in
the code (model/things_table.go): which role is the state and what each
service writes. The state is the state role's reading (on or off for a bool),
`unknown` when it can't be read, and every other role that can be read is an
attribute under its own name: a fan's `percentage`, `preset_mode`,
`oscillating` and `direction`. `toggle` goes by the feedback and is refused
when there is none. A notifier has nothing to read: its state is `unknown`
with `feedback: none`. An update is `on` when what is installed isn't the
latest, and takes no services: HotLoop never installs firmware, because a
failed flash is an outage. A discovered scene is a single-shot button, its
press the scene's payload.

What a thing can be sent is in its attributes, by its config: a thermostat's
`hvac_modes`, `fan_modes`, `preset_modes` and `swing_modes`, a humidifier's
`available_modes`, a water heater's `operation_list`, a fan's `preset_modes`,
a vacuum's `fan_speed_list`
(from the entity's `role_choices` option, which discovery keeps in step with
the config), and the setpoint's `min_temp`/`max_temp` and
`min_humidity`/`max_humidity` (from the tag's range). They're what the screens
offer. They aren't what makes the rule: the gate holds the setpoint to the
tag's range and the driver refuses a word the config doesn't list, whatever an
attribute says. `set_temperature` with none of its three keys is refused, not
a call that does nothing. `turn_on` on a thermostat with no power topic is
refused too, rather than guessing which mode "on" means.

### `light`

On or off by its `state` feedback; `unknown` when that can't be read, and with
no state topic at all, `unknown` for good with `feedback: none`. Brightness is
an attribute, and a JSON-schema light's `color_mode`, `color`, `color_temp`
and `effect` are attributes too: shown, not commanded. `toggle` goes by the
feedback and is refused when there is none to go by.

### `cover`

Its `state` feedback when it has one. With only a position: at or below 1%
`closed`, anything above it `open`. A word that is none of the five is
`unknown`, with `raw_value`. `current_position` is the position when there is
one.

### `event`

An event's state is **when** it last fired (RFC 3339), and `event_type` what it
was; `event_types` lists what it can fire. `unknown` until it has fired since
HotLoop started reading it. It takes no services: nothing commands an event.
Two events in one poll show as the later one; the logbook and the history have
each reading as it came.

## Alarm entities

Every alarm definition is an entity: `alarm.<definition id>` (slugged the same
way a tag's is, so `oven-temp-hi` is `alarm.oven_temp_hi`), platform `alarm`,
`unique_id` `alarm:<definition id>`, named after the definition. It has no
bindings and no device: its state is the alarm engine's, not a tag's, and a
definition does not belong to its device the way a tag does (deleting a device
leaves its alarm definitions). The tag it watches is its `source` attribute.

The state is the ISA-18.2 state the alarm engine holds, spelled the way an
entity state is spelled:

| Alarm engine | Entity state | <span class="sr-only">Details</span> |
|---|---|---|
| `normal` | `normal` | condition clear, nothing outstanding |
| `unack-active` | `active_unack` | condition true, nobody has acknowledged it |
| `ack-active` | `active_ack` | condition true, acknowledged |
| `rtn-unack` | `rtn_unack` | cleared before anybody acknowledged it |
| `shelved` | `shelved` | silenced by an operator, for a bounded time |
| `suppressed` | `suppressed` | silenced by design |

Quality is `good`: the engine's state is not a reading. The entity is
`unavailable` when it is orphaned or the Gateway has no alarm engine. It follows
every transition as it happens, acknowledgements included.

Attributes: `definition_id`, `source`, `condition`, `limit`, `priority` (1 to
4), `priority_label`, `enabled`, `message`, `count`, `active`, `needs_ack`,
`trip_value`, `raised_at`, `cleared_at`, `acked_at`, `acked_by`,
`shelved_until`, `shelved_by`, the last ones present when they apply.

Its services, `acknowledge`, `shelve` and `unshelve`, write no tag, so they do
not go through the write gate. They call the alarm engine's own `Ack`, `Shelve`
and `Unshelve`, the same ones the alarm screen and `POST /api/alarms/{id}/ack`
call, so they land in the alarm trail (`alarm_events`) and the system log
exactly as those do. They need **`alarms.ack`**, not `values.write`: an
operator acknowledges alarms, a viewer does not. A refused call answers 403 and
is logged under the entity with who tried. The call is also one line in the
system log under the entity, with the reason.

`unshelve` is refused (409) on an alarm that is not shelved. The alarm engine
refuses it too, and brings a shelved alarm back in the state its condition is
actually in, not blindly to normal. A service alarms do not take (`turn_on`)
is refused as an unknown service (400) before it goes anywhere near the
engine.

### Platforms with a provider

Alarm entities are the first **provider** platform (`internal/entity/provider.go`):
entities whose source of truth is somewhere other than a tag. A provider says
which entities its platform has right now, renders their state, runs their
services and answers their dry runs; the registry derives, orphans and
re-adopts its entities by `unique_id` exactly as it does a tag's, the state
engine recomputes them on the provider's own events and on its once-a-second
tick, and a service call on one goes to the provider instead of being planned
into tag writes. A provider that writes a tag still writes it through the gate.
The domains and the services each takes are one table
(`model.DomainSpec`), so a platform's new domains are registered in a file of
their own without touching the ones here, which `TestBuiltInDomainsAreUnchanged`
holds byte for byte.

Helpers are the second (`internal/helper`): `input_boolean`, `input_number`,
`input_select`, `input_text`, `input_counter`, `timer` and `schedule`, values
the plant's people own rather than a PLC, kept by HotLoop and set with
`helpers.write`. They write no tag. See [HELPERS.md](/iot/helpers/).

Scripts are the third (`internal/automation`): every script is a `script`
entity, `script.<id>`, on while a run of it is going in any process and off
when none is. `turn_on` runs it with the service data as its fields,
`turn_off` stops it, both with `scripts.run`. Deleting a script orphans its
entity, like deleting an alarm definition. See [SCRIPTS.md](/iot/scripts/).

Recipes are the fourth (`internal/recipe`): every recipe is a `scene` entity,
`scene.<id>`, whose state is when it last wrote to the plant and whose
attributes say how its newest application went. `turn_on` applies it, with
`recipes.apply` and the recipe's own permission when it names one. Deleting a
recipe orphans its entity. See [RECIPES.md](/iot/recipes/).

The sun is the fifth (`internal/sun`): `binary_sensor.sun_up`,
`sensor.sun_elevation` and `sensor.sun_azimuth`, worked out every second from
the site's latitude and longitude, on the box. They read and take no services.
A site with no location has none, and ones left over from when it had one read
unavailable and say which variables to set. See [SUN.md](/iot/sun/).

## Entities everywhere else

### The live feed

`GET /api/stream` carries an `entities` event next to `values`. It is
coalesced the same way, four times a second at most, the newest state per
entity:

```
event: entities
data: {"changed":[{"entity_id":"sensor.press_01_zone1_temp","state":"212.5",...}],"removed":[]}
```

`changed` is the full state of every entity that changed since the last event,
in the same shape as `GET /api/states/{entity_id}`. `removed` is the entity_ids
that no longer have a state at all: disabled, deleted with their device, or
renamed away from (the new name arrives in `changed`). The first `entities`
event on a new connection carries every state, the way `snapshot` carries every
reading, so a screen is populated before anything changes. The `values`,
`snapshot`, `alarm` and `device` events are exactly what they were.

### MCP

Agents get `list_entities`, `get_states` and `call_service`. `call_service`
runs through the same service runner as `POST /api/services/...`, so an agent's
call is gated by the MCP switch like `write_tag` and audited against the entity
with source `mcp`. See [MCP.md](/iot/mcp/#entities).

### Automations

A `state` trigger fires a rule when an entity's state changes, conditions can
read `states`, `attrs` and entity `qualities`, and a `call_service` action
commands an entity through the gate, audited as `automation:<rule-id>`. See
[AUTOMATIONS.md](/iot/automations/#state-triggers-follow-entities).

Both follow the engine's `OnStateChanged` hook, which is why the rules in
[How the engine runs](#how-the-engine-runs) matter: a state trigger sees every
change the engine computes, once, in order, and nothing the engine never saw.

## Screens

**Entities** lists every entity under its place on the equipment tree (its
own place, else its device's), with the tree down the side, and filters by
place, domain, label, text and quality. Inside a place the equipment comes
first (alarms, motors, valves, loops, selects, buttons, counters), then what
can be commanded, then the raw readings.

By default the screen shows each signal once. The entity model gives one
point several entities on purpose, and every one of them keeps its id, but
drawn as tiles that is the same signal two or three times: an armed tag is a
sensor and a switch, and a tag bound into a motor is still its own sensor. On
a real line that roughly doubled the tiles and buried the equipment. So the
screen folds:

- A tag's read entity sits behind its control entity. The switch or number
  is the tile, since it already shows the live state, and its drawer says
  "also available as" with the sensor's entity_id, for whoever is wiring an
  automation or an agent to it.
- A tag bound into a composite sits inside the composite, both its entities.
  The composite's drawer lists its signals: the roles, the tag, what it reads
  now, and its read and control entity_ids. A tag in two composites goes into
  the first by name.
- Only a control or a composite that is neither hidden nor disabled takes
  anything in. Hide or disable the switch and its sensor gets its tile back.
- An alarm on a folded signal flags the tile it is folded into, with the
  alarm's name, and opens the alarm from there. A fold tidies the screen; it
  never hides an alarm.
- The count next to the quality bar says "13 shown · 25 folded", and a tile
  that holds others says so in its foot ("5 signals", "+ sensor"). The
  domain chips, the tree counts and the quality bar count the tiles shown.
- Search and the label filter look inside tiles. Search for an entity_id or
  a tag that is folded and you get the tile that holds it, outlined, with
  "Found in here:" and the entity_id. We picked that over flipping the whole
  screen to every entity: you land on the pump you were looking for, not on
  a wall of tiles.

"Show every entity" turns the fold off and gives every entity its own tile,
for an engineer who wants the raw registry. It is off by default and this
browser remembers it (local storage; a private window forgets it). Nobody
else's screen changes.

States arrive on the live feed's `entities` event; the screen never polls for
them. A tile repaints when its state does, and is repainted even while a
button in it has focus, because a tile that kept an old state for that reason
would be showing the past as the present. Quality is drawn before the value:

| Quality | On screen |
|---|---|
| good | the value, no mark |
| uncertain | the value, an amber edge and an "uncertain" badge |
| bad | the last good value, grayed on a hatch, "bad", and "last good value, reading bad", with the reason after it when the driver gave one |
| no reading yet | "Unknown", in italics, and "reading bad" with the reason when there is one |
| unavailable | "Unavailable", the whole tile hatched |

Controls follow the domain and the role. A viewer sees none. An operator
sees the ones behind `values.write` (and an alarm's behind `alarms.ack`),
disabled with the reason on them when writes are off on this deployment or a
tag the entity writes is not armed. A loop's output is offered only while it
reads manual, because that is the only time the gate allows it. Every command
opens a prompt that says which service, which tags, and what the entity reads
now, and takes a reason for the audit trail. A refusal keeps the prompt open
with the gate's words and every write that did or did not go out. The new
state is never assumed from the command: it comes back on the feed when the
device reads back, or it does not.

The drawer has the state and its timestamps, the controls, an hour, six
hours or a day of the bound tag's history (a step trace, the last value
carried to now, bad readings marked), the other entities of the same signal,
the bindings (for a composite, its signals), the attributes, and every
command made or refused through the entity. An admin also gets the entity_id,
the name, the place on the tree, the labels, hidden and disabled, and delete
for a composite or an orphan.

**New equipment** (admin) builds a composite: pick the domain, name it, and
choose a tag for each role. Each role is offered only tags of a type that fits
it, and a command role shows the tags that are not armed as disabled instead
of hiding them. What is required is marked but not enforced by the form: the
registry decides, and its refusal is shown as it wrote it.

**Plant** is the equipment tree and the labels. See
[EQUIPMENT.md](/iot/equipment/).

## Backup and restore

`entities` and `entity_bindings` are in the backup (`internal/backup.Tables`),
entity_id, customizations and all. That includes composites, every role and
every option, which matters more for them than for anything else: a tag's
entity could be rebuilt from its tag, but nothing can rebuild a composite
except the backup. Alarm entities come back with their definitions, and a
restored definition with no entity gets one on the first sync. A backup taken before this version has
neither table; restore it, start the Gateway, and the registry's first sync
gives every restored tag its entity. `entity_labels` is in the backup too, and
restoring a backup from before the equipment tree is covered in
[EQUIPMENT.md](/iot/equipment/).

Migration 0007 adds three columns to `write_audit`. A backup taken before it
still restores: restore loads a file with fewer columns than today's table into
the leading columns and lets the new ones take their defaults, because a
migration that adds a column always appends it. A backup from a newer version
is still refused. See [BACKUP.md](/iot/backup/).

## What is not here yet

The core, the equipment tree, commanding entities through the write gate,
composite equipment, alarm entities, entities in MCP, automations and the
live feed, and the screens are all here. See [ROADMAP.md](/roadmap/). A state
trigger's `forSec` ("on for five minutes") is in
[AUTOMATIONS.md](/iot/automations/#holding-a-state-forsec).
